text: Boosting libraries have dozens of settings, and it's tempting to throw a giant grid search at all of them. That wastes compute and often buys very little. A better approach: tune in a sensible order, spend most of your effort on the settings that matter, and measure improvements against the noise in your validation scores.

Tune in this order. First, learning rate and number of trees -- they trade off, so fix a moderate rate and let early stopping choose the tree count. Second, tree shape: max_depth and min_child_weight. Third, randomness: subsample and colsample_bytree. Fourth, regularization: reg_lambda, reg_alpha, and gamma. Last, if it matters, lower the rate and retrain with more trees.

Default XGBoost settings, learning rate zero point three, depth six, one hundred trees, scored a test A.U.C. of zero point seven eight eight. Running xgb.cv with a learning rate of zero point one, depth three, and five-fold cross-validation with early stopping settled on fifty-eight trees -- lifting test A.U.C. to zero point eight two seven.

Next, random search samples settings from ranges instead of trying every combination. With twenty-five trials over depth, min_child_weight, subsample, colsample_bytree and reg_lambda, the best trial had depth four, min_child_weight eleven, and reg_lambda about nine point eight, with a cross-validated A.U.C. of zero point eight three four four.

But the honest result: default settings scored zero point seven eight eight test A.U.C., step one with fifty-eight trees scored zero point eight two seven, and the random search scored zero point eight two six -- it did not beat step one. All twenty-five trials scored between zero point eight two six and zero point eight three four mean C.V. A.U.C., while fold-to-fold standard deviation was about zero point zero zero nine.

The ten best trials differed from each other by a standard deviation of only about zero point zero zero zero four -- far below the noise -- so the search couldn't really tell them apart. The big gain came from step one: a sensible learning rate with early stopping and shallow trees. Fine-tuning after that tends to give small, uncertain gains.

Tune on training data only, touching the test set once at the end. Compare every gap against the fold-to-fold noise, and prefer simpler settings when scores tie. Tune in order: rate and tree count first, then shape, sampling, and regularization. Next, we ask when boosting actually beats a random forest.
